newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finnish industry sees milder swings under EMU.
newsitem.headline: Finnish industry sees milder swings under EMU.

text.p: Cyclical fluctuations will be milder, not sharper, in Economic and Monetary Union, the Confederation of Finnish Industry and Employers (TT) said on Wednesday.

"Thanks to EMU, uncertainty about exchange rates in the EU area will be eliminated (and) interest rates and inflation will fall," TT chairman Georg Ehrnrooth told the industrial employer lobby's autumn representatives meeting.
"Cyclical sensitivity will also be reduced by the fact that the Euro will become the world's second biggest invoicing and reserves currency," he said in a copy of a prepared speech. @

"So EMU will of course not make cyclical fluctuations sharper, but milder," Ehrnrooth said, adding it was difficult for the employers' side to understand trade union demands for "new protection mechanisms because of low inflation, stable exchange rates and a low level of interest rates."
Only flawed economic policy, leading to excessive cost pressures and inflation, and to continuing piling up of debt, could create a need for exceptional buffer arrangements, he said.
"Do we need to protect ourselves against ourselves?" Ehrnrooth asked.
"EMU is of course not an easy alternative because it will impose a new kind of discipline on us," he said.
The best buffers against cyclical downturns were strong state finances and foreign exhange reserves together with strong corporate balance sheets.

Addressing other union concerns linked to EMU, Ehrnrooth said joining the single currency would not undermine the Finnish collective wage bargaining system nor would it automatically entice companies to go for nominal wage cuts as a first buffer against cyclical downturns.
EMU would also boost employment, he said.
"The intention of EMU is to increase, not reduce, the competitiveness and profitability of Europe's economies and companies and so promote employment," Ehrnrooth said.
He later told a news conference that staying outside EMU would have "a negative impact on our interest rates ... and on our willingness to invest."
"We are supporting EMU and we think it is important for Finland to be among the first countries to join," he said.
The buffer funds demanded by unions were "alien to us," Ehrnrooth said.
